segments.text: Hello everyone and welcome to this lecture on  HTTP methods and Adam potency. In this video we
will understand the five most commonly used HTTP  methods that is get, post, put, patch and delete.
We will learn how these methods help a client  communicate its intention clearly to a server
and how each method represent a specific type  of action that can be performed on a resource.
We will also explore an important concept  called IDEM potency. Now the concept may
sound technical at first but the idea behind is  quite simple. So understanding Adam potency help
us design APIs that behave reliably even when  the request are accidentally repeated because
of network issues or user actions. So let's get  started with understanding the HTTP methods.
So whenever a client sends a request to a  server, it is usually trying to accomplish one
of the two things. The client may want to retrieve  information such as viewing a product or checking
an order status. Alternatively, it may also want  to create, update, or remove information that is
stored on the server. Now, HTTP methods provide  a standard way for the client to tell the server
exactly what type of action should be performed  on the resource. As we discussed in our earlier
lectures, a resource can be almost anything that  the system manage. It could be a customer profile,
a product, a order, a shopping cart or even a  payment record. So by looking at the HTTP method,
the server immediately understand what the client  want to do with that resource. Now let's examine
all these five commonly used HTTP methods and try  to understand their purpose. So first one is get
method. This method is actually used whenever  a client want to retrieve information from the
server. The primary purpose of get request is  to read data without changing anything. So when
a server receive a get request, it look for  the requested resources and sends its current
information back to the client in an agreed  format. For example, let's say we have an online
shopping application. So where a customer open  a product page to view a pair of shoes. Now the
application sends a get request to the server. Now  server locate the product information and return
details such as product name, price, description,  available size and images. So if the customer
refresh the page or view the same product multiple  times, the product itself remain unchanged. So
simply viewing information does not modify the  resource at all. So in nutshell the get request
only retrieve information. they are considered  read only operations. Now let's talk about the
post method. So unlike get the post method is used  when the client want to create something new. When
the server receive a post request, it typically  create a new resource and store it in the system.
For example, when a customer add a product to  their shopping cart, then in that case application
may send a post request to the server and server  will process the request and create a new cart
item associated with that customer. Similarly,  when a customer place a new order, the application
will send a post request because it is completely  a new order and it must be created in the system.
Now you should always remember that in case if  you send the same request multiple time then the
server will end up creating multiple resources.  So let's say we have a customer who accidentally
tap the same button twice. Then in that scenario  server will end up creating the second resource
without knowing that the first resource is already  present. So in such scenarios your business logic
should be smart enough that it should not trigger  the second request with similar customer details.
Right now let's talk about our next method that is  put method. So this method is used when the client
want to replace an existing resource completely.  So instead of sending only the information that
has changed, the client will send the entire  resource representation and server will use
this information to replace the existing record  which is present on the server. For example,
imagine a customer that moves to a different city  and needs to update their shipping address. Now,
in this case, the application can send a  put request containing the complete address
information including the street, city, state, and  postal code. When the server receive this request,
it will replace the previous address with the  new address that is supplied by the client.
Now in other words, put actually treats the  incoming data as the new complete version of
the resource. So in nutshell, you use put method  whenever you want to replace or update the entire
resource. Now let's talk about our next method  that is patch method. So patch is used when an
only part of a resource need to be updated. Right?  So that means like you already have a resource and
you want to update any specific information on  that. So instead of sending the entire resource
detail again the client send only a specific  attribute that needs to be changed. For example,
suppose a customer want to update only their phone  number while keeping every other part of their
profile exactly the same. So in this situation  sending the complete profile information would not
be required. Instead, the application can send a  patch request containing only the new phone number
and the server will update the individual field  while keeping all other information untouched.
So this approach actually reduce the amount of  data that is being transferred and make update
more efficient. So as a result patch is commonly  used for small targeted modification to existing
resources. Now let's talk about our final method  that is delete method. As the name suggests the
delete method is used when the client want to  remove a resource from the system. Now when
the server receive a delete request, it actually  locate the specific resource and remove it. So for
example, if a customer decide that they no longer  want a particular item in their shopping cart.
So in that situation the application will send a  delete request for that cart item. Now the server
will process the request and remove the item  from the cart and after the item has been removed
it is no longer available within the resource  collection. So delete method is used to provide
a standard and a consistent way for clients  to request the removal of data or resources.
Now so far we have discussed all the key HTTP  methods. Now let's talk about the term IDM potency
or the concept. So at first glance the term Adam  potency may sound complicated but the underlying
concept is straightforward. It simply asks one  question. If the exact same request is sent
multiple times will the final result remains  the same or it will continue to change. Now
this question become important in the real world  systems because request are not always delivered
perfectly. Network interruptions, temporary  server issues and user actions can sometimes
cause the same request to be submitted more than  once. So as an API designer, we need to understand
how our system behaves in such situations. So  let's look at all these HTTP methods from the
perspective of IDOM potency. So let's start with  get method. So suppose a customer open the same
product page 10 times. Each get request will ask  the same product information and each request will
return the same resource. So the act of reading  the information does not modify the resource. So
essentially repeating the request does not change  the final state of the system and that is why get
is considered as it imputed. Now let's talk  about our next method that is put method.
So in this case, let's say the client is sending  the same shipping address update multiple times.
So regardless of how many times the request  is repeated, the address stored on the server
will remain exactly the same. So essentially the  final result does not change irrespective of how
many requests you are sending. So put is also  considered as it put in. Now let's talk about
the delete. So when a delete request is sent to  delete item from the cart or maybe any record
from the server. So essentially system will going  to drop or delete that record. Now if you issue
the same request again to delete item. So in that  case there is nothing to delete from the card. So
eventually server might respond with a different  response code but the final state of the resource
does not change. And due to this fact only delete  is also considered as a important. Finally let's
consider patch. So patch is generally treated  as a important when it updates a field to a
specific value. For example, if a request set  a customer phone number to a particular number,
then repeating the same request multiple times  will still produce the same final result. as
long as the update do not depend on how many times  it has been applied. So batch is also considered
as a important. Now let's talk about the post  method which actually behaves differently from
other method that we have discussed so far. So  whenever a post request is processed successfully,
a new resource is usually created. For example,  imagine that a customer submit an order creation
request. If the same post request is accidentally  sent three times, then server may end up creating
three separate orders. Because each request can  create an additional resource, the final state
of the system continue to change with every  request. Right? And for this reason, post is
generally considered as nonadam potent. At this  point, you might be wondering why Adam potency is
so important. Now the answer is that it directly  affect how reliable and predictable a system
behaves in the real world. Imagine a customer  using the Meridian Commerce website to place an
order. Now let's say customer internet connection  is slow and after clicking the place order button
there is no response immediately on the screen.  Now customer assumes that the click did not work
and press the button again. If the order creation  process rely on a post request and no safeguard
exists to prevent duplicate request then system  may end up creating two separate orders and charge
customer twice. So this is exactly the type of  problem that a solution architect must anticipate
during system design instead of customer being  charged twice and then they are reporting the
issue. So understanding Adam potency actually help  architects identify the risk and build mechanism
that will prevent unintended outcome during the  entire process. Let's bring all these HTTP methods
together using a single business scenario. Let's  say a customer begin by browsing products in the
meridian commerce catalog and each time customer  view a product the application send a get request
to retrieve product information. When the customer  decide to purchase an item the application send
a post request to create a new order. Later on,  if the customer move to a different address and
want to replace their complete shipping  information, the application will send a
put request with all the updated details. If the  customer only want to add a delivery instruction
such as leave the package at the front door, the  application can send a patch request containing
just specific changes. Finally, if customer  want to cancel the order before shipment, the
application will send a delete request to remove  the order from the processing queue. This example
actually demonstrate how each HTTP method has a  distinct purpose and contribution to a clean and
predictable API design. So before we wrap up this  video, here's a brief summary of what all we have
discussed. First, get is actually used to retrieve  information without changing anything. Post is
actually used to create a new resource. Put is  actually used to replace an entire resource with
a new version of the data. Patch is used to modify  only part of a resource. Delete is used to remove
a resource. Now from an item potency perspective,  get, put, patch, and delete generally produce the
same final result even if you're sending the same  request. Whereas post can create a new resource
every time it is executed and is therefore not  an important method. So to conclude, HTTP methods
provide a clear and standardized way for client  and server to communicate. They allow a client
to express whether it want to retrieve, create,  update or remove a resource. It potency actually
help us understand how the system behave when  the same request is repeated multiple times. This
becomes extremely important in distributed systems  where retry network delays and accidental update
actions are very common. So together HTTP methods  and IDMP potency help solution architects and
developers design API that behaves consistently,  reliably and predictably under real world
scenarios. So far if you have any question then do  write that in the comment section and we're going
to provide answer after this video. In case if  you like this video then hit the like button and
